newsitem.title: USA: Low bank reserves no issue for Fed policy--NY Fed.
newsitem.headline: Low bank reserves no issue for Fed policy--NY Fed.

text.p: The sharp decline in commercial banks' reserve balances at Federal Reserve banks has resulted in greater volatility in the federal funds rate but is unlikely to affect the conduct of monetary policy, a New York Fed official said on Tuesday.

"I don't think it is possible to foresee some critical level of reserves below which the conduct of monetary policy would not be effective," New York Fed senior vice president Paul Bennett told Reuters.
Bennett was commenting on the decline in recent years of the reserves that bank are required to maintain at the Fed.

The decline stems from "sweeps" or the now common practice by commercial banks to move customers' funds from accounts that require to maintain reserve balances against them into accounts that are exempt of reserve requirements.

The "sweeps" practice has resulted in commercial banks maintaining increasingly lower reserves, leading private analysts to question whether the Fed would find it difficult -- or eventually impossible -- to implement interest rate changes in such environment.

"Since the Federal Reserve implements monetary policy by influencing the federal funds rate, and the funds rate affects other short-term interest rates, a large increase in its volatility could have broader implications," Bennett said.
"But it does not look that it's going to be a problem. The banks have to manage their own reserve balances. They do so in a fashion that is consistent with monetary policy," he added.

Bennett, who described the decline in bank reserve volume as "a transition that is working smoothly," wrote a paper on the topic with New York Fed assistant vice president Spence Hilton. It appears in the New York Fed's "Current Issues."
The declining trend in reserves was sparked by the Fed's decision in the early 1990s to eliminate reserve requirements on some deposits or lower them on others.

But Bennett acknowledged "the most influential factor lowering required balances recently has been the growth of sweep account arrengements," that resulted in a drop in required reserve balances to just $11.5 billion in February 1997 from $29.4 billion in late 1993.
Such decline has been accompanied by "an apparent upward tilt in federal funds rate volatility in the past year," Bennett noted.
"The mechanisms have changed somewhat but the substance (of monetary policy) is pretty much the same," the New York Fed senior vice president further said in an interview.
"Reserves are still relevant (to monetary policy). Banks will continue to use their accounts with the Fed because that's how they do business with each other," Bennett added.
"As long as we are making it transparent to the public what we are aiming for, this will not affect the conduct of monetary policy in any substantitve way," he also said.
"To date, significantly lower balance requirements have not interfered with the smooth functioning of the federal funds market," Bennett concluded.
The Fed last set the funds rate at 5.50 percent on March 25.
